items.prompt: What is information architecture?
choices: How content and features are organized, labeled and connected so people can find them
How the colors, fonts and spacing of a site are chosen to look polished and modern
How the database tables behind a site are named and indexed for speed
items.explanation: IA is the map: structure, labels and links that let people reach things.

items.prompt: What is a mental model in this unit?
choices: How the engineering team draws the system architecture on a whiteboard
How the search index ranks results for a typed query
How a person naturally groups and names things before seeing your site
items.explanation: It is the visitor's own grouping, formed before they meet your menu.

items.prompt: What is an implementation model?
choices: How a card sort is run with a group of participants
How the company stores, staffs or builds things internally
How a visitor expects things to be grouped when they arrive
items.explanation: Warehouse departments, tables and org charts are all implementation models.

items.prompt: Why could Trailhead's shoppers not find the rain jacket?
choices: The nav followed warehouse departments, not what shoppers were doing
The jacket photo was too small to see clearly on mobile screens
The checkout page failed whenever a jacket was added
items.explanation: The product existed and worked; the map to it did not match the shopper's thinking.

items.prompt: What was NOT wrong with the Trailhead site?
choices: The grouping used by the top-level menu labels
The match between nav labels and shopper goals
The jacket page itself, its photo and its price
items.explanation: The page was fine. The structure leading to it was the problem.

items.prompt: A grocery store files shelves by supplier contract. What do shoppers expect?
choices: Shelves sorted by the alphabet of each supplier's name
Fruit, bread and cleaning supplies grouped as they think of them
Shelves sorted by which supplier delivers on which weekday
items.explanation: Shoppers use their own categories, not the store's purchasing ones.

items.prompt: Which question does the fix start from?
choices: How would someone looking for this describe it?
How do we store this in the warehouse most cheaply?
How many clicks can the developers build this in?
items.explanation: Start from the visitor's description, then translate the storage map.

items.prompt: Which is a sign of a findability problem?
choices: A nav bar that contains more than one word per label
A site that loads quickly on every device type
Support tickets asking for things the product already has
items.explanation: People asking for existing features is the classic symptom of a bad map.

items.prompt: Where do mental models come from?
choices: The order in which the developers shipped each page
People's own experience and goals, before they see your menu
The labels the company printed on its warehouse shelves
items.explanation: They exist in the visitor's head regardless of your structure.

items.prompt: A bank's menu has 'Ledger Services' and 'Retail Products', matching its internal divisions. A customer cannot find how to dispute a charge. What is the best diagnosis?
choices: The dispute page itself is poorly written and needs clearer wording about refunds
The internal division names leaked into the nav, so it follows the bank, not the customer's task
The bank needs more top-level menu items so every division gets its own entry and landing page
The customer should be using the search box instead of the menu for this task
items.explanation: The nav mirrors the organization. The customer is thinking about a task, not a division, so the label gives them no scent to follow.
items.reference:
Two maps of the same shop
🧠 mental model: shopper groups by what they are doing (hiking)
🏭 implementation model: company groups by how it stocks (apparel)
👀 the nav should show the first, built from the second
Why: a nav that copies the company's internal grouping makes the visitor learn the company before they can shop.
items.learnMore:
Mental model vs implementation model

Both groupings can be tidy and consistent. IA fails when the internal one leaks straight into the nav instead of being translated into how visitors think.

Common mistake

Believing a consistent, tidy tree must be a findable one. Consistency with the company's storage says nothing about the visitor's expectations.
items.reflection: Think of an app or form you use that is organized by how the company works rather than what you want to do. What would you rename or regroup first?

items.prompt: A team says: 'Our nav is perfectly consistent, every product has exactly one home.' Why does that not show the nav works?
choices: Every product should in fact have two homes so that no single path can ever fail for any kind of visitor
A consistent nav always loads slowly because each page must check its category rules
Consistency with the company's own storage says nothing about whether visitors expect those homes
Consistency only matters for search, and has no bearing on browsing a menu at all
items.explanation: A tidy implementation model can still be a bad visitor model. The test is a match with how people think.

items.prompt: Which nav is the clearest example of an implementation model leaking into the interface?
choices: Top-level sections named after the three internal teams that maintain them
Sections named after the task a visitor is trying to complete on arrival
Sections that were validated by letting people sort cards into piles first
Sections that include a fallback path for visitors who already know the name
items.explanation: Team names are a fact about the org chart. The other options are driven by visitor behaviour.

items.prompt: A redesign changes colors, fonts and photos but leaves the same warehouse-based menu. Findability barely moves. Why?
choices: Fonts and colors always reduce findability, so the redesign made things worse
Photos replace menus, so the menu was never used by visitors in the first place
Findability is decided only by the server response time of the category pages
The structure and labels people have to guess through were never changed at all
items.explanation: Visual design polishes the page. Findability is decided by the map, which stayed the same.

items.prompt: What is a taxonomy?
choices: The set of categories and the rules for what belongs in each
The color scheme applied to category pages across a site
The list of search words typed by visitors last month
items.explanation: Taxonomy is the buckets plus the membership rules.

items.prompt: What is a hierarchy?
choices: A ranking of products from cheapest to most expensive
A list of every page sorted by the date it was published
How the categories nest inside one another, like a tree
items.explanation: The hierarchy is the nesting, not the list of buckets itself.

items.prompt: What is cross-listing?
choices: Listing a product on a competitor's site as well as yours
One item reachable from more than one valid branch
Copying a product into the warehouse twice to be safe
items.explanation: One real product, several legitimate paths in.

items.prompt: In a deep and narrow tree, a visitor has...
choices: Few choices per screen but many levels to get through
Many choices per screen but only a level or two
No choices at all until after they have used search
items.explanation: Narrow means few choices per level; deep means many levels.

items.prompt: In a shallow and wide tree, a visitor has...
choices: Few choices per screen but many levels to click
A single path with no choices to make along the way
Many choices per screen but only a level or two
items.explanation: Wide means many choices per level; shallow means few levels.

items.prompt: Rain jackets appear under Hiking, Climbing and Camping. How much inventory is that?
choices: Zero products, since it is only a menu label
One product, reachable by three paths
Three separate products that each need stock
items.explanation: Cross-listing changes the map, not the stock.

items.prompt: In the unit's model, what does each extra level add?
choices: A fixed click cost plus a scan cost for that screen
Nothing, since only the number of choices matters
A cost that shrinks to zero once a visitor is logged in
items.explanation: Levels multiply the per-level cost, so depth hurts fast.

items.prompt: In the model, what does adding choices to a level do?
choices: Doubles scan time for every choice that is added
Leaves the time unchanged however long the list gets
Raises scan time slowly, since people scan in chunks
items.explanation: The scan cost grows with the log of the choices, so it rises slowly.

items.prompt: Which is the model's find time at 4 choices per level, 3 levels deep?
choices: About 9.0 seconds
About 3.9 seconds
About 1.3 seconds

items.prompt: A single jacket really suits both hiking and climbing, and the team wants to pick the branch it belongs to 'most'. What happens if they do?
choices: Search stops indexing the jacket because it now has only one category
Visitors who arrive thinking of the other activity have no path to it
The product page loads slowly since it must look up its single home
The warehouse must move the jacket to match the menu branch it was given
items.explanation: Forcing a winner swaps 'no path' for 'the only path is the wrong one' for half the visitors.
items.reference:
One product, several doors
🌳 taxonomy: the buckets and their rules
📊 hierarchy: how buckets nest (breadth x depth)
🚪 cross-listing: one product page, more than one path in
⏱️ model: 4 x 3 levels = 3.94 s, 8 x 2 levels = 3.22 s (64 products each)
Why: a product that serves two reasons for shopping needs two paths in, and the shape of the tree changes how many decisions a visitor must survive.
items.learnMore:
Hierarchy, cross-listing and tree shape

A tree has breadth (choices per level) and depth (levels). In the unit's simple model each extra level adds a fixed click cost, while extra choices add a small scan cost, so shallow-and-wide beats deep-and-narrow until a single screen gets too crowded.

Common mistake

Treating cross-listing as duplicated inventory. It is one product page with several paths in; the real cost is keeping every path's breadcrumbs and filters current.
items.reflection: Think of something you own that genuinely belongs in two places (a tool, a book, a file). Where do you look first, and what would a second path in cost you to maintain?

items.prompt: In the model, a 4-choice by 3-level tree and an 8-choice by 2-level tree both reach 64 products. Which finds faster, and why?
choices: The 8 by 2 tree, 3.22 s to 3.94 s, with one fewer fixed click cost
The 4 by 3 tree, because each screen is smaller and scanning dominates the time
They tie at 64 products, because reachable count alone decides the find time
The 4 by 3 tree, because logarithms make more levels cheaper than extra choices
items.explanation: Each level costs a fixed 0.5 s plus its scan; removing a level saves more than the wider scan adds.

items.prompt: The model says 12 choices at depth 1 takes 1.80 s, much faster than 4 by 3. Why not just make every menu one flat screen?
choices: A flat screen cannot show more than three items on a phone, whatever the model says
The model is wrong for flat screens because logarithms are undefined at depth 1
One level of 12 reaches only 12 items, so large catalogs still need more depth
Flat menus are always slower in practice because visitors click each choice in turn
items.explanation: Reach is choices to the power of levels. Speed in the model is bought with a small catalog.

items.prompt: A manager objects: 'Cross-listing the jacket in three branches means three copies of the jacket.' What is the best reply?
choices: It is three real copies, but the extra stock is cheap compared with the sales gained
It is zero cost because cross-listing is purely visual and never needs updating
It is a cost only the search index bears, so the nav team can ignore it
One product page with three paths in, so the cost is upkeep of each path
items.explanation: Inventory is unchanged. Maintenance of every path is the real price of cross-listing.

items.prompt: Which navigation is visible on every page?
choices: Global navigation
Local navigation
Contextual navigation
items.explanation: Global is the always-visible bar.

items.prompt: Which navigation exists only inside one section?
choices: Global navigation
Contextual navigation
Local navigation
items.explanation: Local navigation, like a section's filter sidebar, stays inside its section.

items.prompt: Which navigation appears only where it is relevant to one item?
choices: Local navigation
Contextual navigation
Global navigation
items.explanation: A 'pairs well with trekking poles' link belongs to one product page.

items.prompt: Which label is accurate but internal?
choices: Hardgoods
Camping
Hiking
items.explanation: 'Hardgoods' is correct industry jargon a shopper never uses.

items.prompt: Which label is too ambiguous to narrow anything down?
choices: Camping
Tents
Gear
items.explanation: 'Gear' covers everything, so it helps no one choose.

items.prompt: Which label best matches what the visitor is trying to do?
choices: Category 4
Camping
Hardgoods
items.explanation: A task-aligned label is the one visitors recognize.

items.prompt: Search works best when the visitor...
choices: Can name what they want
Does not know what exists yet
Wants to see every category
items.explanation: Search rewards a known name.

items.prompt: Browse works best when the visitor...
choices: Types an exact product code from a receipt
Only wants the single most popular item
Knows their situation but not the product name
items.explanation: Browse suits 'something for a rainy hike'.

items.prompt: Why does a site need both search and browse?
choices: Search always replaces the need for categories
They fail in opposite situations
Browse is a backup that is rarely used
items.explanation: Visitors who know the name and those who do not need different tools.

items.prompt: A visitor searches 'raincoat' and gets zero results, though the shop sells 'shell jackets'. What is the problem and the fix?
choices: A search vocabulary mismatch, fixed with a raincoat and shell jacket synonym
A hierarchy problem, fixed by moving shell jackets to the top level of the menu
A labeling problem in the global bar, fixed by renaming 'Hiking' to 'Raincoats'
A browse problem, fixed by removing search so everyone uses the menu instead
items.explanation: The visitor never opened a menu. The failure is the index not matching their word, so restructuring the tree would not help.
items.reference:
Where each piece lives, and how it fails
🧭 global: every page (top bar)
📂 local: inside one section (filters)
🔗 contextual: tied to one item (pairs well with...)
🏷️ label test: would an outsider recognize it?
🔍 search fails on vocabulary; browse fails on missing branches
Why: each part answers a different question, so a fix to one never replaces the others.
items.learnMore:
Navigation, labels, search and browse

Global navigation follows you everywhere, local navigation belongs to one section, and contextual links belong to one item. Labels pass when an outsider recognizes them. Search needs the visitor's word to match yours; browse needs a branch that matches their situation.

Common mistake

Putting a section-specific filter in the global bar, or investing only in search. Each puts the right control in the wrong place, or covers only one of the two ways people look.
items.reflection: Think of a site where you typed a word and got nothing, even though the thing existed. What word did the site use, and how would you have found it by browsing?

items.prompt: A shop puts 'Men's / Women's / Kids' filters in the always-visible top bar. What is the mistake?
choices: A global control was placed in contextual navigation, hiding it from most visitors
A local control sits in the global bar, cluttering pages it does not suit
A contextual link was used as a label, which makes it meaningless to outsiders
A search feature was placed in the menu, so browse visitors cannot see it
items.explanation: Those filters only make sense on category pages, so they belong to local navigation.

items.prompt: In an open card sort, participants...
choices: Invent their own pile names
Sort cards into your fixed categories
Rate how much they like the homepage
items.explanation: Open means the categories come from the participants.

items.prompt: In a closed card sort, participants...
choices: Invent their own pile names from scratch
Click through a finished website design
Sort cards into categories you already proposed
items.explanation: Closed means you supply the categories.

items.prompt: Which sort suits the early stage, when the mental model is unknown?
choices: Neither, since sorts need a finished site
Open card sort
Closed card sort
items.explanation: Open sorts reveal the shape of the model.

items.prompt: Which sort suits late validation of a draft taxonomy?
choices: Closed card sort
Open card sort
Neither, since validation needs analytics
items.explanation: A closed sort tests a specific proposal.

items.prompt: What does a card sort produce?
choices: One correct grouping that all participants agree on
A pass or fail verdict for the whole website
A distribution of how people grouped the cards
items.explanation: It is signal across participants, not a single right answer.

items.prompt: What does a tree test give participants?
choices: A set of cards and a blank table to fill
A task and only the menu tree, with no visuals
A full design with photos and promotional banners
items.explanation: Only the text tree and a task.

items.prompt: Why does a tree test hide photos and banners?
choices: So visual design cannot rescue a weak structure
Because photos make the test take longer to run
Because banners are not allowed to be tested
items.explanation: It isolates the structure from the visuals.

items.prompt: In the story, 82% of participants made a 'Hiking' pile with the jacket. What does that suggest?
choices: The jacket should be removed from the shop entirely
The word Hiking should be banned from the labels
The taxonomy should have a Hiking branch that reaches it
items.explanation: A strong grouping is a strong signal for a branch.

items.prompt: Which method measures whether people can finish a real task in the tree?
choices: Color contrast check
Tree test
Open card sort
items.explanation: The tree test is the task-completion check.

items.prompt: Tent stakes score 88% in the tree test under the old 'Hardgoods' nav. What should the team conclude?
choices: The label works well, so the whole Hardgoods branch should be copied into the new design
Tents sitting nearby may explain the score, so it says little about the label
The tree test is unreliable, so its other results should all be ignored as well
Stakes should be moved to the top level, because high scorers deserve a better position
items.explanation: A tree test measures the whole path. Adjacency to tents can explain success without the label meaning anything.
items.reference:
Two tests, two questions
🗂️ card sort: how do people group these items? (mental model)
🌲 tree test: can people finish a task in this tree? (structure)
📊 result is a distribution, not one right answer
🚫 tree test shows no photos or banners: structure only
Why: a card sort reveals the grouping people expect; a tree test checks whether a given tree lets them complete real tasks.
items.learnMore:
Card sorts and tree tests

Open sorts let people invent piles and names, best early. Closed sorts use your categories, best to validate. A tree test gives a task and only the text tree, so visual design cannot rescue a weak structure.

Common mistake

Reading a good score as proof the label works. A path can succeed because of where things sit nearby, not because the label meant anything to the visitor.
items.reflection: Think of a structure you built yourself (folders, a shelf, a project board). How could you test it on someone else without explaining it first?

items.prompt: A team has a draft tree and wants to know if people can find things in it. Which method fits?
choices: A tree test using real tasks and the draft tree
An open card sort with blank piles
A survey asking people to rate the nav's look
An analytics dashboard of last year's page views
items.explanation: The question is task completion in a proposed structure, which is what a tree test measures.

items.prompt: 61% of participants also put the rain jacket in a 'Climbing' pile. How should the team read that?
choices: As noise to discard, because only the largest pile should decide the placement
As proof that 'Hiking' is a wrong label that must be replaced right away
As a cross-listing signal, since many people independently see two valid homes
As a sign that the sort was run badly, since people should agree on one pile
items.explanation: Overlapping homes across participants are exactly what cross-listing exists to serve.

Card sorts and tree tests

Open sorts let people invent piles and names, best early. Closed sorts use your categories, best to validate. A tree test gives a task and only the text tree, so visual design cannot rescue a weak structure.

Common mistake

Reading a good score as proof the label works. A path can succeed because of where things sit nearby, not because the label meant anything to the visitor.
items.reflection: Think of a structure you built yourself (folders, a shelf, a project board). How could you test it on someone else without explaining it first?

items.prompt: A tree test is run with hero photos and sale banners shown beside the menu. What goes wrong?
choices: Nothing, since photos always make participants take the test more seriously
The test becomes a card sort, because banners act as piles of related items
Participants are unable to click any branch while a banner is on screen
Visuals can rescue a weak tree, so the result no longer isolates the IA
items.explanation: The test is meant to measure structure alone. Extra cues blur whether the tree or the visuals did the work.
items.reference:
Two tests, two questions
🗂️ card sort: how do people group these items? (mental model)
🌲 tree test: can people finish a task in this tree? (structure)
📊 result is a distribution, not one right answer
🚫 tree test shows no photos or banners: structure only
Why: a card sort reveals the grouping people expect; a tree test checks whether a given tree lets them complete real tasks.

items.prompt: Why did the redesign keep 'Shop by product type'?
choices: Some visitors already succeeded that way
Because the old nav was deleted by mistake
Because search cannot index product types
items.explanation: Removing a working path trades one problem for another.

items.prompt: What did the redesign mainly change, according to the unit?
choices: How deep the tree is, from three to six levels
How many photos each product page shows
How well the labels matched the mental model
items.explanation: Breadth barely moved; alignment did.

items.prompt: What is the cost of cross-listing an item?
choices: Extra payment fees on every sale made through it
Extra breadcrumbs and filters to maintain
Extra stock that must be bought for each branch
items.explanation: More paths mean more upkeep.

items.prompt: What does it mean that taxonomies rot?
choices: A bucket that fit a small catalog can overflow as it grows
The category names slowly turn into random characters
Old pages are deleted automatically by the server
items.explanation: 'Hiking' at 200 SKUs can become 'Hardgoods' at 2,000.

items.prompt: Why does a label that suits one audience risk failing another?
choices: Labels are only valid in one language at a time
Labels cannot be changed once a site goes live
A beginner may not call themselves a hiker yet
items.explanation: Self-classification differs between visitors.

items.prompt: For a catalog of about 200 SKUs, which structure usually works?
choices: No categories at all and no search
3 or 4 top-level branches
Over 100 top-level branches
items.explanation: Small catalogs need few branches.

items.prompt: What does a catalog of 20,000 SKUs usually need?
choices: Facets and heavier use of search
Only three equal buckets and nothing else
A single scrolling page of every product
items.explanation: No shallow hierarchy stays both browsable and useful at that scale.

items.prompt: What is a SKU?
choices: A single page of the website's menu
A kind of search filter
One sellable inventory item
items.explanation: Often one product in one size and color.

items.prompt: When should an IA be re-tested?
choices: Only when the company changes its logo
After the catalog grows or changes a lot
Never, since a redesign is permanent
items.explanation: Re-testing is part of maintaining an IA.

items.prompt: The redesign deletes 'Shop by product type' to force everyone through the activity menu. What is the likely outcome?
choices: Visitors who succeeded by product type lose a working path
Search gets faster because it has fewer categories to cover
The tree test results for diagnosed products drop to zero
Cross-listing stops working because branches must be unique
items.explanation: The tree test flagged only some products as broken. Removing a working route fixes one group by breaking another.
items.reference:
What a redesign has to protect
✅ fix the diagnosed products: rain jackets, trekking poles
🛣️ keep working paths: 'Shop by product type' stays as a fallback
🔁 cross-listing costs maintenance on every extra path
📈 200 SKUs over 3 branches: about 67 each; 20,000 over 4: 5,000 each
🕰️ re-test as the catalog grows
Why: a fix aimed at one mismatch can create another if it removes a route that already worked for someone.
items.learnMore:
Trade-offs in a redesign

The smallest change that fixes the diagnosed products is usually better than a total rebuild. Keep working paths as secondary routes, accept the maintenance cost of cross-listing knowingly, and plan to re-test as the catalog grows.

Common mistake

Assuming the redesign is permanent. A bucket that fit 200 products can become a dumping ground at 2,000, just as 'Hardgoods' did.
items.reflection: Think of a system you reorganized that worked for a while and then slowly filled up again. Which part of the old structure would you have kept?

items.prompt: Trailhead's catalog grows from 200 to 20,000 SKUs. Why do 3 or 4 activity branches stop working?
choices: Four branches is the maximum the nav can display on any screen size
Each branch would hold about 5,000 items, which is no longer browsable
Activity labels become illegal once a catalog has more than 10,000 SKUs
Each branch would hold under 10 items, so the menu becomes too sparse to use
items.explanation: 20,000 over 4 branches is 5,000 each. Large catalogs need facets and search to cut that down.

items.prompt: A redesign flattens and widens the tree but keeps the internal label 'Hardgoods'. What is likely to happen to findability?
choices: It improves a lot, because shallower trees always beat better labels
It gets worse, because wide menus are slower than deep ones in every case
It stays poor, since the label-to-mental-model gap was never closed
It improves only on mobile, because labels are hidden on small screens
items.explanation: The unit's redesign worked because labels matched the mental model; tree shape barely changed.

items.prompt: Two years after the redesign, 'Hiking' holds 2,000 products. What does this show?
choices: The redesign was wrong from the start and should never have used activities
Cross-listing caused the growth, so it should be switched off for every item
The card sort data was invalid, since 'Hiking' should never get so many items
The fix has a shelf life, so the IA must be re-tested as the catalog grows
items.explanation: A bucket that fit 200 items can become the next dumping ground; re-testing is ongoing maintenance.
